title: A / an, the and zero article 3

sections.title: With plural and uncountable nouns
sections.content:
With plural and uncountable nouns, zero article is used to talk generally, without definite people or things in mind. The is used when we are referring to specific people or things. Compare:
• The government has promised not to tax books. (= books generally) and The books have arrived. (= the books you ordered)
• Music played an important part in his life. (= music generally) and I thought the music used in the film was the best part. (= that particular music)

sections.title: Holidays, times of the year, days
sections.content:
We often use zero article with the names of holidays, special times of the year, months, and days of the week including Easter, Ramadan, New Year's Day. But compare:
• I'll see you on Saturday. (= next Saturday)
• We met on Saturday. (= last Saturday)
• They came on a Saturday as far as I can remember. (= a day of the week, not which particular Saturday)
• They came on the Saturday after our party. (= a particular Saturday)
With winter, summer, spring, autumn, and New Year (meaning the holiday period), we can use either zero article or the:
• In (the) summer I try to spend as much time as I can in the garden.
We use the when it is understood or we go on to specify which summer, spring, etc. we mean:
• I'd like to go skiing in the autumn. (= this year)
When we want to say that a particular holiday, season or period of time was somehow special, we can use It / That was ... + a / an + noun + modifying phrase. Compare:
• That was a winter I'll never forget. (= compared to other winters it was unforgettable)
• That was the winter we went to Norway. (= a statement about a particular winter)

sections.title: Times of day and night
sections.content:
We use zero article with times of the day and night such as midnight, midday, and noon:
• If possible, I'd like it finished by midday.
But note that we can say either the dawn or dawn.
We use the + morning / afternoon / evening for a day which is understood or already specified:
• I enjoyed the morning, but in the afternoon the course was boring.
But compare:
• Morning is the time I work best. (= mornings in general; The morning is also possible)
• I'll be there by (the) morning / evening. (but ... by the afternoon, not ... by afternoon)

sections.title: by + zero article
sections.content:
We use by + zero article with some verbs to talk about means of transport and communication. Compare:
• I generally go by bus to work. and I generally take the bus to work.
Also: go / travel by car / taxi / bus / plane / train / air / sea; contact / communicate by post / email / phone

exercises.question: ___ as young as ten are working in the clothing industry.
exercises.hint: Use zero article for plural nouns in a general sense.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Children
Use zero article for plural nouns in a general sense. Article choice depends on whether the noun is specific/known to the listener ('the') or introduced for the first time ('a/an').

exercises.sentence: She went to the school this morning to speak to the head teacher.
exercises.correction: She went to the school this morning to speak to the head teacher.
acceptable: She went to the school this morning to speak to the head teacher.
exercises.hint: Visitor going to a specific school building → 'the school' is correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She went to the school — CORRECT
'The school' is correct here because she went as a visitor to a specific building, not as a student or teacher. Compare: 'She went to school' (as a student — zero article, general purpose) vs 'She went to the school' (to visit the specific building as an outsider).
exercises.prompt: Is this sentence correct? If not, rewrite it correctly.

exercises.question: While you're painting the sitting room, I'll take ___ over to the park.
exercises.hint: Use 'the' for specific children (e.g., our children).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: the children
Use 'the' for specific children (e.g., our children). The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: He was taken to a hospital after the accident and kept overnight for observation.
exercises.correction: He was taken to hospital after the accident and kept overnight for observation.
exercises.hint: Going to hospital as a patient → zero article (British English).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: taken to hospital (British English)
In British English, 'go to hospital' (zero article) means as a patient or for treatment — the institution is used for its primary purpose. 'Go to the hospital' refers to the specific building as a visitor. This pattern applies to: school, university, college, church, prison, court, hospital, bed. American English typically uses 'the hospital'.

exercises.question: I've been working in the garden all ___ afternoon and my back aches.
exercises.hint: We typically say 'all afternoon' without an article.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: zero article
We typically say 'all afternoon' without an article. Article choice depends on whether the noun is specific/known to the listener ('the') or introduced for the first time ('a/an').

exercises.question: After university, she went to ___ sea and spent three years working on merchant ships.
exercises.hint: 'Go to sea' = become a sailor / work at sea → zero article.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: sea (zero article)
'Go to sea' means to take up a life at sea or work as a sailor — zero article. Compare: 'The sea was calm' (a specific body of water — definite article) vs 'He went to sea at 18' (the occupation/way of life — zero article). Similar: 'go to work', 'go to bed', 'at home', 'in town'.

exercises.question: A: Can you remember when we last saw Alex? B: It was ___ Sunday in June, I think.
exercises.hint: Use 'a' when referring to a day of the week, but not which particular one.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: a
Use 'a' when referring to a day of the week, but not which particular one.

exercises.question: I got ___ from Carla yesterday. B: How is she now?
exercises.hint: When 'email' means a single message, it is a countable noun taking 'a/an'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: an email
When 'email' means a single message, it is a countable noun taking 'a/an'. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.
